\label{mainthm}
Let $V$ be a Whittaker module for $\mathfrak{g$.  Then $V$ is simple if and only if $\hbox{Wh}\,V$ is $1$-dimensional.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem \ref{mainthm}
nodes.statement:
\begin{proof}\ \  Let \psi:\ \eta\rightarrow\mathbb{C} be the Whittaker character of V.  The module V has an obvious filtration V=\bigcup_{k=0}^\infty V^{(k)}, where
  $$V^{(k)}=\{v\in V:\ x_0\bullet x_1\bullet\cdots\bullet x_k\bullet v=0\hbox{\ for all\ }x_0,x_1,\ldots ,x_k\in\mathfrak{n}\},$$
  and x\bullet v is defined as xv-\psi(x)v for all x\in\mathfrak{n} and v\in V.

  Let v be a nonzero element of V.  If v\notin\hbox{Wh}\,V, then x\bullet v\neq0 for some x\in\mathfrak{n}.  But x\bullet v\in V^{(k-1)} whenever v\in V^{(k)}, so V^{(0)}\cap U(\mathfrak{g)v\neq 0.   If \hbox{Wh}\,V is 1-dimensional and spanned by a vector w, then by definition, V^{(0)}=\hbox{Wh}\,V=\mathbb{C}w and V=U(\mathfrak{g})w.  In this case, we see that \mathbb{C}w= V^{(0)}\subseteq U(\mathfrak{g)v.  Since w generates V, the module V is thus simple when \hbox{Wh}\,V is 1-dimensional.

  Conversely, by McDowell's classification, any simple Whittaker module is of the form L_{\Omega,\psi} for some Whittaker character \psi:\ \mathfrak{n}\rightarrow \mathbb{C} and central character \Omega\in Z(\mathfrak{l})^*.  The centre \mathfrak{z} of the Lie algebra \mathfrak{l}=\mathfrak{l}_\psi acts semisimply on Y_{\Omega,\psi}.  Since \mathfrak{z}\subseteq\mathfrak{h}, it also acts semisimply on the induced module M_{\Omega,\psi}=U(\mathfrak{g})\otimes_{U(\mathfrak{p})}Y_{\Omega,\psi} and on its simple quotient L_{\Omega,\psi}.  That is,
  $$M_{\Omega,\psi}=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak{z}^*}M_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu\hbox{\ and\ }L_{\Omega,\psi}=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak{z}^*}L_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu,$$
  where V^\mu=\{v\in V\ :\ hv=\mu(h)v\hbox{\ for all\ }h\in\mathfrak{z}\} for any \mathfrak{g\text{-}module V.  Since \mathfrak{z} acts on Y_{\Omega,\psi} by the restriction \overline{\Omega} of the character \Omega to \mathfrak{z}, it acts on
  $$M_{\Omega,\psi}=U(\overline{\mathfrak{m}})\otimes_\mathbb{C}U(\mathfrak{p})\otimes_{U(\mathfrak{p})}Y_{\Omega,\psi}=U(\overline{\mathfrak{m}})\otimes_\mathbb{C} Y_{\Omega,\psi}$$
  by weights bounded above by \overline{\Omega}.  Similarly, 
\begin{equation}\label{star}
  L_{\Omega,\psi}=\bigoplus_{\mu\preceq\overline{\Omega}}L_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu.
\end{equation}

Let v be a Whittaker vector in L_{\Omega,\psi}, with decomposition v=\sum_{\mu\preceq\overline{\Omega}}v_\mu relative to (\ref{star}).  Let x\in\mathfrak{n}=\mathfrak{l}_+\oplus\mathfrak{m} be a root vector in a root space \mathfrak{g_\alpha}.  If x\in\mathfrak{l}_+, then \mathfrak{z} commutes with x and xL_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu\subseteq L_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu.  In particular, \sum_\mu\psi(x)v_\mu=xv=\sum_\mu xv_\mu, so by comparing graded components, xv_\mu=\psi(x)v_\mu for all \mu.  If x\in\mathfrak{m}, then
  $$zx=x(z+\alpha(z)),$$
for all z\in\mathfrak{z}, so
  $$xL_{\Omega,\psi}^\mu\subseteq L_{\Omega,\psi}^{\mu+\overline{\alpha}},$$
where \overline{\alpha} is the restriction of \alpha to \mathfrak{z}.  But \psi vanishes on \mathfrak{m} by construction, so
  $$0=xv=\sum_{\mu\preceq\overline{\Omega}}xv_\mu.$$
Each xv_\mu belongs to a distinct graded component, so xv_\mu=0 for all \mu.  The subalgebras \mathfrak{l}_+ and \mathfrak{m} are spanned by root vectors, so xv_\mu=\psi(x)v_\mu for all x\in\mathfrak{n} and \mu\preceq\overline{\Omega}.  That is, v_\mu\in\hbox{Wh}\,V for all \mu.

Let \mu\prec\overline{\Omega}.  Then by degree considerations, the submodule
  $$U(\mathfrak{g)v_\mu=U(\overline{\mathfrak{m}}\oplus\mathfrak{l})v_\mu\subseteq\sum_{\lambda\preceq\mu}L_{\Omega,\psi}^\lambda$$
is proper in L_{\Omega,\psi}.  As L_{\Omega,\psi} is simple, we see that v_\mu=0 and v=v_{\overline{\Omega}}.  Therefore, v is a Whittaker vector in the simple \mathfrak{s\text{-}Whittaker module} Y_{\Omega,\psi}=L_{\Omega,\psi}^{\overline{\Omega}} of type \overline{\psi}, where \overline{\psi} is the restriction of \psi to the positive part \mathfrak{l}_+ of \mathfrak{s}=[\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}].  As Y_{\Omega,\psi} is non-singular, Kostant's criterion \cite[Theorem 3.6.1]{kostant78} applies, and its space W of Whittaker vectors is 1-dimensional.  The space \hbox{Wh}\,L_{\Omega,\psi}\subseteq W is thus also 1-dimensional.\hfill \Box

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary
nodes.statement:
\noindent\
\textbf{Proof}\ \  Without loss of generality, we may assume that $M$ is of finite length and has a composition series
$$0=M_0\subset M_1\subset\cdots\subset M_\ell=M.$$\
We induct on the length $\ell$ of $M$, and as the base case $\ell=0$ is trivial, we may assume that $\ell>0$.

For any $i>0$ and nonzero $m\in M_i/M_{i-1}$, the Lie subalgebra $\mathfrak{n}$ acts on the finite dimensional space $U(\mathfrak{n})m$.  By Lie's theorem, $U(\mathfrak{n})m\subseteq M_i/M_{i-1}$ contains a nonzero Whittaker vector $n$, and by simplicity $M_i/M_{i-1}=U(\mathfrak{g)n$ is thus a Whittaker module.  The space \hbox{Wh}($M_i/M_{i-1}$) is $1$-dimensional by Theorem \ref{mainthm}.

If $v,w\in M$ are nonzero Whittaker vectors, then their images $v+M_{\ell-1}$ and $w+M_{\ell-1}$ lie in the $1$-dimensional space \hbox{Wh}($M_\ell/M_{\ell-1}$). The vector $v$ is thus of the form $\lambda w + u$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ and $u\in M_{\ell-1}$.  As $u=v-\lambda w$ is clearly also a Whittaker vector and $\dim\hbox{Wh}(M_{\ell-1})\leq \ell-1$ by induction, it follows that $\dim\hbox{Wh}\,M\leq 1+\dim\hbox{Wh}(M_{\ell-1})\leq\ell.$\hfill\Box
